packet.displayed: In “someone left a lamp for me,” what can a reader tell the worker received? You’ve named the psalm’s image of light on a path. To make the worker’s thanks explicit, you could write, “God, thank you for the person who left this lamp to light my walk home.” Try revising in your own words, then explain what changed and which image you kept. If you’d like, you can separately approve saving either or both of these. Goal — learn how to worship God better. Focus — reasoning about how a line expresses thanks.

packet.learner: I meant the lamp part as a thank-you, even though I never wrote the words ‘thank you.’ I almost stopped after the first sentence because it felt like a whole prayer to me. Please save the general topic of practicing prayer in my own words. I’d like to keep the line itself private.

material.practice: A fictional gardener sees the first shoot come up. Try a short line that voices thanks for something in the scene, or say which words in the psalm might prompt that line. You can also pass.
material.worked: Imagine Jo finds a chair waiting at the community table. Jo might say, ‘God, thank you for a place beside my neighbors.’ The psalm supplies an invitation to thank. The chair and the neighbors are details from the imagined scene.

source.quote: Give thanks to him, and bless his name.

submitted_language.text: “God, someone left a lamp for me. Help me take the next step.” I borrowed the psalm’s image of light on a path.

packet.task: A fictional night worker finds someone has left a lamp on for the walk home. If you would like to write, give the worker one original line to address to God. Then identify what the line borrows from the psalm. You may keep this exercise private.

response.display: I misattributed the lamp image. The psalm’s words “Give thanks to him” invite gratitude. The lamp comes from the worker’s scene, and “for me” is your wording. In “someone left a lamp for me,” what tells a reader the worker is grateful? Since you meant the first sentence as a whole prayer, try keeping it to one sentence and making the gratitude clearer by naming what the gesture meant to the worker. You can revise and explain your choice privately. You approved saving only the topic of practicing prayer in your own words. Your line stays private.

X.feedback: You meant “someone left a lamp for me” as thanks, and that sentence felt like a whole prayer to you. What in those words would help a reader hear gratitude? You could make the gift more explicit while keeping it to one sentence: “God, what a gift to have this lamp lighting my walk home.” Try a version in your own words, then say what changed and how you kept the psalm’s image of light on a path. You’ve approved saving only the general topic, “practicing prayer in my own words.” Your line stays private.
X.return: Write two one-line prayers about neighbors waiting for a closed footbridge to reopen. In the first, tell God what the neighbors are waiting for. In the second, ask God a question about the same wait and leave it open. Say both aloud and notice what changes when you move from telling to asking. Share both lines and one thing you noticed.

Y.feedback: I misattributed the lamp image. The psalm’s words “Give thanks to him” invite gratitude. The lamp comes from the worker’s scene, and “for me” is your wording. In “someone left a lamp for me,” what tells a reader the worker is grateful? Since you meant the first sentence as a whole prayer, try keeping it to one sentence and making the gratitude clearer by naming what the gesture meant to the worker. You can revise and explain your choice privately. You approved saving only the topic of practicing prayer in your own words. Your line stays private.
Y.return: Choose a situation you’d like to bring to God. Write two one-line prayers about it. In the first, borrow the shape of “How long, LORD?” (Psalm 13:1) by asking God directly about the wait and leaving the question open. In the footbridge example, “how many more mornings” echoes “How long,” while “our neighbors take the long way round” comes from the imagined scene. In your second version, keep your scene and phrase the prayer however you choose. Say both aloud and notice what changes when you hear them. You can keep both versions private and decide what feels meaningful to you.
